CO2016A-GE-21.exp: The passage says 'The well-mannered person interacts with everyone in the same polite manner, regardless of age, sex, class, gender or religion' and 'does not discriminate'. So social inferiors are addressed no differently from anyone else.

CO2016A-GE-22.exp: The passage instructs: 'Do not get agitated if one does not agree with you or when you disagree with others.' Monopolising and interrupting are behaviours the passage expressly forbids.

CO2016A-GE-23.exp: To 'monopolise' is to take exclusive possession or control of something - here, of the whole conversation, leaving no room for others. The board game Monopoly is only a play on the word.

CO2016A-GE-24.exp: The passage says of criticism: 'Do it in a polite and civilised manner.' Voice, tone and quietness are not what the text specifies.

CO2016A-GE-25.exp: 'Encroaching' means intruding or trespassing beyond proper limits, and it appears in the passage's list of polite actions: 'not encroaching on their personal space'. 'Amass' means to accumulate and 'offensive' means insulting, so neither fits.

CO2016A-GE-26.exp: The passage glosses the proverb in the very next sentence: 'It is good manners that define us as civilised persons.' The saying means manners are what make a person civilised, not that manners merely reveal character.

CO2016A-GE-27.exp: The passage links the two ideas directly: 'living in society is not an easy job. There are social codes of conduct to be followed if one is to live in civilised society.' The difficulty lies in having to observe those codes.

CO2016A-GE-28.exp: The passage states 'Nobody is born with inherent good manners. Everyone either learns or acquires them', so 'acquired' is the direct opposite of the rejected 'inherent'. Imitation and teaching are only the means by which they are acquired.

CO2016A-GE-29.exp: Per the passage, the well-mannered person 'interacts with everyone in the same polite manner, regardless of age, sex, class, gender or religion'. Option C is precisely what the passage rejects, since 'He does not discriminate'.

CO2016A-GE-30.exp: The passage concludes that to be considered respectable 'he first has to treat others in a respectable manner'. It expressly denies that wealth earns respect: 'One may amass great wealth or fame, but if his manners are unpleasant, he does not command respect.'

CO2016A-GE-31.exp: The passage explains 'we are judged by the way we speak because it is a good indicator of our character and personality' and 'How we speak ... reflects our personality.' The reason given is what speech reveals, not whom we meet.

CO2016A-GE-32.exp: The closing line reads: 'By cultivating good manners, one can thereby, become the person that he wishes to be.' Treating others respectfully and being civilised are consequences of good manners rather than the stated means.

CO2016A-GE-33.exp: 'Jumped over the wall' is the idiomatic collocation, 'over' expressing movement across and clear of an obstacle. 'Above' describes static position without crossing, and 'upon' would mean landing on top of the wall.

CO2016A-GE-34.exp: The adjective 'indifferent' takes the preposition 'to' - indifferent to something means unconcerned about it. 'Indifferent about' is a common but non-standard substitution.

CO2016A-GE-35.exp: 'Preparation' is followed by 'for' when naming the event one is getting ready for: preparation for the function. 'Preparation of' would mean the making of the thing itself.

CO2016A-GE-36.exp: 'Faith' collocates with 'in' - to have faith in a person or a decision. 'Faith with' and 'faith of' are not standard English.

CO2016A-GE-37.exp: 'Ran over' is the fixed phrasal verb for a vehicle knocking down and passing across a victim. 'Ran into' would mean collided with, which does not suit a puppy under a car.

CO2016A-GE-38.exp: 'Within' is the preposition used with a period of time to mean before that period ends - within this week. 'By' normally needs a point in time ('by Friday', 'by the end of this week') rather than the whole week, so 'within' is the better fit with the emphatic 'itself'.

CO2016A-GE-39.exp: Taking the underlined word to be the final 'that', it is a demonstrative pronoun standing in for 'that phone' - a pronoun, not a conjunction. Confidence is low because the underlining was lost when this question was extracted, and 'much' (adverb) or 'better' (adjective) would each give a different answer.

CO2016A-GE-40.exp: Taking the underlined word to be 'Poverty', it is an abstract noun and the subject of the sentence. The underlining was lost in extraction, but three of the sentence's words are nouns while only 'is' (verb) and 'huge' (adjective) offer alternatives, and no word in it is an adverb.
